sentences.text: Yingshanosaurus was a medium-sized, slow-moving quadrupedal herbivore that lived in what is now Southwestern China. It measured between four and five meters in length.

The exact purpose of Yingshanosaurus's osteoderms is a subject of debate among scientists, though researchers suggest the plates may have been used for display, species recognition, or thermoregulation.

The skeleton includes nine dorsal vertebrae, a sacrum consisting of five firmly fused vertebrae, and five nearly complete osteoderms from various body regions. The largest osteoderm is an 80 cm long parascapular spine from the shoulder. The transverse processes of the vertebrae project at an angle of about 60 degrees relative to the neural spine. Yingshanosaurus possessed seven haemal arches with typical stegosaur anatomy, differing from the inverted T-shape of Kentrosaurus. Four sacral vertebrae were solidly fused with the ilium of the pelvis. The animal had medium-height neural arches, and the neural spines of its dorsal vertebrae were plate-shaped with a transversely expanded top.
Early reconstructions incorrectly placed Yingshanosaurus's large shoulder spines near the pelvic girdle as 'parasacral spines' before Gigantspinosaurus clarified their position.
The genus name Yingshanosaurus is derived from the locality of Yingshan, while the species name refers to the location of the locality, Jichuan.

A partial skeleton was discovered in 1983 when a villager in Jichuan, Sichuan Province, China, found it while digging a house foundation. A stegosaur skeleton was excavated in Sichuan in 1983 by a team led by Wan Jihou, and the discovery was reported by Zhou Shiwu in 1984.

The only known species, Yingshanosaurus jichuanensis, was named and described in 1994. Zhu Songlin formally described the genus and species in 1994, designating the skeleton as holotype specimen CV00722.
Like all stegosaurs, Yingshanosaurus was a herbivorous dinosaur.
Zhu noted that the femur-to-tibia ratio of Yingshanosaurus is more similar to Kentrosaurus than to Stegosaurus or Dacentrurus.
Zhu classified Yingshanosaurus within the family Stegosauridae and the subfamily Stegosaurinae. The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Yingshanosaurus as Stegosauridae.

Fossils of Yingshanosaurus come from the Upper Shaximiao Formation, dating to the Bathonian age of the Jurassic. Early estimates in 2011 placed the age of Yingshanosaurus fossils in the Middle Jurassic, specifically the Bajocian to Bathonian stages. Later research established the Bathonian stage as the oldest possible age for the Upper Member of the Shaximiao Formation where Yingshanosaurus was found. Yingshanosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 155 million years ago in the Kimmeridgian stage. The Paleobiology Database records the time range of Yingshanosaurus as the Bathonian to Callovian stages, between 168.2 and 161.5 million years ago.

Some researchers argue the name should be considered invalid because the original description was difficult to find. It was assumed for a long time that the name Yingshanosaurus would remain a nomen nudum due to insufficient description, despite the conference being published in 1986. Although the validity of the name has been reaffirmed, it is rarely cited in international scientific literature.
